strengths: Addresses an important problem: reducing the cost of Monte Carlo integration when a hierarchy of fidelity levels is available. The resulting estimator is intuitive and compatible with score-based control functionals for unnormalized densities. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/iclr2026--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-nhqsnu4x/call-7fecabca7cbe47f4b3372986f697f666/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}
The conditional unbiasedness argument is plausible for independent held-out samples, and the paper derives a cost-constrained allocation from its variance upper bound.
The evaluation spans synthetic integration, differential equations, Bayesian inference, and variational inference, with comparisons to MLMC, control functionals, and MLBQ.
The appendices provide proofs, sample allocations, kernel formulas, and some kernel and sampling-design sensitivity experiments.
weaknesses: The methodological novelty is limited: MLCF is essentially the direct application of an existing control-functional estimator to each term of the standard MLMC telescoping sum. The theory largely combines an existing control-functional approximation bound with a standard allocation calculation, without adequately distinguishing the contribution from broader multifidelity control-variate approaches.

The theoretical claims are overstated. Exact RKHS membership, quasi-uniform training designs, Stein boundary conditions, common smoothness, and independent i.i.d. evaluation samples are strong assumptions. Several experiments explicitly violate them, while the variance proof also drops cross-level covariance without clearly assuming independence across levels.

The claimed superiority over single-level CF is not established generally: the discussion following Equation 7 assumes unproved RKHS-norm inequalities. Moreover, the proposed allocation requires unknown constants and RKHS norms; outside the tailored synthetic example, the experiments instead use the MLMC allocation.

The budget comparisons omit Gram-matrix construction and cubic solves, kernel-hyperparameter optimization, score evaluations, and sampling costs. With sample counts up to 620 and simulator budgets below one second, this omitted overhead could dominate, undermining the central efficiency claim.

The variational-inference evidence is particularly weak. With one sample, the simplified CF estimator in Equation 11 algebraically reduces to that sample, so the headline MLCFRG experiments contain no actual control-functional variance reduction. The closest MLMCRG baseline is essentially tied and is slightly better for the 20-unit network. Proposition 3.4 is derived for plain SGD, whereas the experiments use Adam, so its recurrence, variance bound, and computational-saving claims do not directly apply.

The stated mixed derivative of the Matérn-5/2 kernel omits the dimension factor: the leading radial term in the trace should contain d times the displayed expression. This is incorrect for the two-dimensional synthetic experiment and raises concerns about either the implementation or reproducibility.

Key experimental details are missing, including reference values used to compute absolute errors, some fidelity step sizes, MCMC chain and effective-sample-size diagnostics, cross-level coupling, kernel regularization values, and the wine-data subset, split, and preprocessing. The MCMC experiment also uses dependent samples despite the main guarantee requiring i.i.d. evaluation points.

The strongest synthetic test is deliberately constructed inside the same RKHS used by the estimator and is only two-dimensional. There is no convincing scaling study over dimension, number of levels, conditioning, or model mismatch, and the limited replication/statistical analysis does not support the broad applicability claims.

strengths: The level-wise combination of Stein control functionals with the MLMC telescoping decomposition is intuitive and potentially useful for expensive multifidelity integration.
The paper provides an unbiased split estimator, a conditional variance bound, a closed-form sample-allocation rule, and implementation details.
Experiments span synthetic integration, differential equations, Bayesian inference, and variational inference, with comparisons against MC, MLMC, CF, and MLBQ.

The manuscript is organized and visually polished, and no significant ethical concern is apparent. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/iclr2026--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-vl6nt6b5/call-b6f11e31d1bb4835a31fc894f45ecc7d/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}
weaknesses: The novelty is limited: the estimator applies existing control functionals independently to standard MLMC increments, while the main proofs combine a prior CF interpolation bound with standard allocation arguments. The theory does not establish general conditions under which MLCF beats CF; both have the same budget exponent, and the claimed constant-factor advantage relies on unproved comparisons between norms in different RKHSs.

There is a major theory-experiment disconnect. The guarantees require independent levels, i.i.d. evaluation samples, quasi-uniform training designs, strong RKHS smoothness, and favorable dimension, whereas experiments use MCMC, QMC/LHS, high-dimensional BNNs, and nonsmooth ReLU networks. The manuscript itself acknowledges that assumptions fail in several experiments.

The experimental estimator is not identified clearly as the split unbiased estimator (Eq. 4) or the biased simplified estimator (Eq. 11), and no training fraction is reported. In the BNN experiments, MLCFRG uses one sample: Eq. 4 cannot then be formed, while Eq. 11 algebraically reduces to the raw sample and is independent of the kernel. Consequently, these experiments do not demonstrate a control-functional benefit; results are also tied with, and for hidden size 20 slightly worse than, MLMCRG.

The equal-budget comparisons appear to count integrand evaluations but omit Gram-matrix construction/inversion, repeated marginal-likelihood tuning, score evaluation, and memory. Since the reported model evaluations cost only milliseconds, these omitted costs may dominate, undermining the central efficiency claim.

Important reproducibility details are missing, including actual fidelity step sizes for the ODE and Lotka-Volterra studies, construction of reference values used for absolute error, MCMC initialization/mixing/ESS, dataset subsampling and splits, and exact regularization and hyperparameter-optimization protocols.

There are technical inconsistencies: the stated multidimensional Matérn mixed derivative appears to omit factors of dimension; the per-level marginal-likelihood expression has a log-determinant sign/coefficient inconsistent with the preceding objective; the variance proof sums levels without explicitly assuming cross-level independence; and the VI argument conditions away the random optimization history, treats vector gradients through scalar variance notation, and derives an SGD update while experiments use Adam.

strengths: The manuscript addresses an important problem and presents an intuitive, modular combination of Stein control functionals with MLMC corrections. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/iclr2026--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-hz_gk3fq/call-3c85a9594a5241ce8c3ca527d4c58c7e/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}
The split-sample construction is unbiased under the required Stein and independence conditions, and the paper derives a conditional variance bound and a corresponding allocation formula.
The empirical section covers several settings, including synthetic integration, differential equations, an unnormalized Bayesian posterior, and variational inference.
The appendices report proofs, kernels, sample allocations, and some implementation details, and the paper acknowledges cubic kernel cost and dependence on smoothness.
weaknesses: The central algorithm is a largely direct composition of two established techniques: apply an existing control-functional estimator independently to every term of the standard MLMC telescoping sum. The variance result mostly sums known single-level bounds, so the methodological novelty is limited.

The theoretical assumptions are far from mild and exclude most showcased applications. In particular, the finite fill-distance condition is impossible on R^d, while the Gaussian, posterior, and BNN examples have unbounded support; QMC, LHS, and MCMC experiments also do not satisfy the i.i.d. holdout assumptions. Assumption A7 does not even cover the level-zero term as written.

There are substantive technical problems. The stated mixed derivative of the Matérn-5/2 kernel omits a dimension factor and is only correct in one dimension, despite a two-dimensional synthetic experiment. The per-level marginal-likelihood formula has the wrong sign/factor for the log-determinant term. Proposition 3.4 drops the randomness and covariance of the recursive gradient history; its bound is only conditional, and the claimed full adaptive-trajectory guarantee is not established.

The claimed superiority over ordinary CF is not proved: it relies on unassumed comparisons between RKHS norms and costs. Likewise, the proposed allocation depends on unknown interpolation constants and RKHS norms; it is demonstrated only on a synthetic integrand constructed from the same kernels, while practical experiments revert to MLMC allocation.

Experimental budgets appear to omit Gram-matrix solves, repeated hyperparameter optimization, and score-function computation. These costs can dominate when model evaluations take only fractions of a millisecond, so the reported fixed-budget comparisons do not support end-to-end efficiency claims.

Crucial experimental details are missing, including which unbiased or biased MLCF estimator is used, the training/test split ratio, the Lotka-Volterra reference value used for absolute error, MCMC convergence and effective sample size, and whether score-evaluation costs are included.

The variational-inference evidence does not validate the control-functional contribution. With the stated one-sample setup, the simplified estimator in Eq. 11 reduces algebraically to the raw one-sample increment; if additional fitting samples were used, they are undocumented and uncosted. Moreover, Table 6 has MLCFRG performing slightly worse than the existing MLMCRG baseline on both metrics, contradicting the broad outperforming claim.

The evaluation lacks end-to-end runtime and scaling studies, dimensionality or smoothness ablations, statistical significance analysis, and competitive modern control-variate baselines. Overall, the evidence is insufficient for the paper's broad applicability and efficiency claims.

strengths: The core idea is elegant and useful: apply Stein-based control functionals separately to the telescoping increments of multilevel Monte Carlo, avoiding handcrafted control variates and supporting unnormalized target densities.

The paper derives an unbiased sample-split estimator, a conditional variance/convergence bound, and a cost-constrained sample allocation that exposes the roles of smoothness, dimension, fidelity discrepancy, and evaluation cost.

Experiments span synthetic integration, a boundary-value ODE, real-data Lotka–Volterra inference, and Bayesian-neural-network variational inference. Comparisons include MLMC, CF, MLBQ, MCMC variants, and useful kernel/design/allocation studies; the low-dimensional integration results consistently favor MLCF.

The manuscript is well organized, visually polished, and unusually candid about computational and regularity limitations; the appendix provides substantial mathematical and implementation detail. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/iclr2026--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-w_dkqu72/call-425e83ec3fec460a9638ef587b8314a1/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}
weaknesses: The novelty is somewhat incremental: the construction applies an existing single-level control-functional estimator independently to standard MLMC increments, and much of the analysis follows by summing an existing CF bound and optimizing it with a Lagrange multiplier. Positioning against broader multifidelity and scalable Stein-control-variate methods is not strong enough to establish a major conceptual advance.

The theoretical assumptions are restrictive and poorly aligned with the principal experiments. The global fill-distance condition cannot hold for finite designs on the unbounded Gaussian/posterior domains used, NUTS samples are not i.i.d., exact RKHS membership is strong, and independence across levels is used but not clearly assumed. Consequently, the advertised faster rate does not cover the Bayesian examples or the 392/522-dimensional BNN setting.

The claimed comparison showing the MLCF bound below the CF bound assumes, without justification, inequalities between RKHS norms defined using different level-specific kernels. Moreover, the proposed optimal allocation depends on unknown constants and RKHS norms and is validated only on a synthetic integrand constructed to make those norms available; practical experiments instead use the MLMC allocation.

The efficiency evaluation counts fidelity-model evaluations but omits Gram-matrix inversion, repeated marginal-likelihood tuning, score computation, and posterior-sampling costs. This is particularly consequential when the coarse level uses up to 620 points despite subsecond evaluation budgets. End-to-end wall-clock and memory scaling could materially change the comparisons.

The variational-inference extension is under-supported. Proposition 3.4 is only a conditional variance statement for an SGD recurrence and does not establish optimization convergence for adaptive parameters or the Adam experiments. The main BNN experiments use one MLCFRG sample; with one point, the simplified CF estimator in Equation 11 reduces to the raw function value and therefore cannot demonstrate benefit from the control-functional component. Table 6 also slightly favors MLMCRG over MLCFRG.

Important reproducibility details remain absent or ambiguous, including the ODE and Lotka–Volterra level step sizes, construction and uncertainty of the reference integrals used for absolute error, MCMC warm-up/ESS and replication protocol, BNN subsample and train/test split, numerical regularization values, and whether each experiment uses the unbiased estimator in Equation 4 or the biased simplified estimator in Equation 11.

strengths: The central construction is intuitive and potentially useful: applying Stein-based control functionals separately to the terms of an MLMC telescoping sum combines multifidelity modeling with nonparametric variance reduction and permits unnormalized target densities through score evaluations.

For the independent split-sample setting, the paper provides an unbiased estimator, a conditional variance bound under explicit smoothness and fill-distance assumptions, and a cost-constrained sample-allocation formula.

The empirical study spans synthetic integration, differential equations, Bayesian inference, and variational inference, and includes comparisons with MC, MLMC, CF, and MLBQ as well as limited kernel and experimental-design sensitivity analyses.
weaknesses: The conceptual and theoretical novelty is modest: the estimator and its variance proof largely apply an existing control-functional result independently to each MLMC term. No rigorous condition establishes improvement over single-level CF or MLMC; the discussion asserting B_MLCF < B_CF relies on unproven inequalities between RKHS norms and costs.

There is a substantial theory-to-experiment mismatch. The main guarantees require independent evaluation samples, quasi-uniform training designs, RKHS membership, boundary conditions, and sufficiently dense samples, whereas experiments use QMC, LHS, MCMC, high-dimensional adaptive optimization, and apparently the biased all-sample estimator. Bias is not quantified, and cross-level independence and MCMC dependence are not addressed.

The variational-inference evaluation is particularly problematic. With only one MLCFRG sample, the unbiased split estimator cannot be constructed; if the simplified estimator in Eq. (11) is used, it algebraically reduces to the raw function value and is independent of the kernel, while a pairwise-distance median heuristic is undefined. The reported tables show MLCFRG essentially tying MLMCRG and performing slightly worse in the 20-unit case. Moreover, the proposed recursion is derived for SGD but experiments use Adam, and the unconditional dependence across optimization iterations is not covered by the stated variance proof.

The efficiency comparison excludes control-functional construction, Gram-matrix inversion, hyperparameter optimization, and score computation from the reported budgets. Given the cubic kernel cost and millisecond-scale model evaluations in the experiments, this omitted overhead may dominate; no end-to-end wall-clock or memory comparison supports the efficiency claims.

Reproducibility is insufficient despite the paper's statement to the contrary. Missing or unclear details include how reference integrals are obtained, the train/evaluation split and value of rho, ODE and Lotka-Volterra level step sizes, MCMC warmup and diagnostics, the Lotka-Volterra time horizon and observations, and the BNN subset and data split. Statistical uncertainty is shown only partially, without paired tests or confidence intervals for claimed improvements.

Several concrete mathematical inconsistencies further reduce confidence: the stated Matérn-5/2 mixed-divergence formula omits dimension-dependent factors, the ODE forcing changes from -50^2 x_2^2 to +50 x_2^2 during its derivation, and the two supposedly equivalent marginal-likelihood objectives have incompatible log-determinant signs/scalings. The claims of mild assumptions and broad applicability are also overstated, especially for the 392- and 522-dimensional BNN examples where the rate suffers severely from dimension.

There is a substantial gap between theory and experiments. The bound requires quasi-uniform training designs, i.i.d. evaluation samples, and finite fill distance, whereas key experiments use unbounded Gaussian/posterior domains, MCMC, QMC, and LHS. The appendix admits that assumptions are violated. Cross-level independence is also needed for the sum-of-variances proof but is not stated clearly.

The practical estimator used in the experiments is unclear because training sizes m_l and train/evaluation splits are never reported. QMC/LHS experiments appear to require the biased simplified estimator in Eq. (11), but its bias is neither characterized nor separated from variance. Consequently, the main theorem does not directly explain the reported results.

The proposed allocation depends on unknown smoothness, RKHS norms, and level-dependent constants r_l. The claim that r_l can be normalized away is unjustified when kernels differ across levels. Exact allocation is demonstrated only on a synthetic example constructed from the same RKHS; all realistic experiments instead reuse the MLMC allocation.

The budget comparisons omit the method's score evaluations, Gram-matrix construction and cubic solves, and repeated kernel-hyperparameter optimization. These costs may dominate the millisecond-scale simulators used in the experiments. No end-to-end runtime or scaling comparison is provided, so the central efficiency claim is not established.

The variational-inference evidence is particularly weak. The main MLCFRG experiments use one sample, for which the simplified control-functional estimator in Eq. (11) algebraically reduces to the raw sampled correction and provides no control-functional variance reduction. Results are essentially tied with MLMCRG and are worse in Table 6. Moreover, Proposition 3.4 relies on a plain-SGD parameter update, while the experiments use Adam, and the vector-valued extension of the scalar variance theory is not developed.

Several concrete inconsistencies impede reproducibility: the Matérn mixed-derivative formula omits dimension-dependent factors, the per-level marginal-likelihood objective has a log-determinant sign/scaling inconsistent with the preceding joint objective, and the ODE forcing changes sign or magnitude between its definition and discretization. Reference values for absolute errors, MCMC diagnostics, and important BNN dataset/preprocessing details are also missing.

strengths: The paper addresses an important problem: reducing the cost of Monte Carlo integration when a useful hierarchy of model fidelities is available.

Applying a Stein control functional independently to each MLMC correction is simple and modular. The split-sample estimator has a plausible unbiasedness argument when training points are fixed and evaluation samples are independent.
The manuscript derives a variance bound and a budget-allocation rule that expose the roles of smoothness, dimension, fidelity cost, and inter-level discrepancy.
The experiments span synthetic integration, differential equations, Bayesian inference, and variational inference, with relevant CF, MLMC, and MLBQ comparisons.
weaknesses: The methodological novelty is modest: the central estimator is essentially MLMC with an existing control-functional estimator applied separately to every correction. Its improved convergence exponent is inherited from prior control-functional theory, while the multilevel construction primarily changes constants.

The theoretical guarantees require strong RKHS-membership, smoothness, quasi-uniform fill-distance, and independence assumptions. They do not cover the unbounded Gaussian domains, MCMC samples, high-dimensional ReLU BNNs, or biased full-sample estimator used in the applications. Cross-level independence is also used in the variance proof without being stated.

The claimed practical allocation requires unknown approximation constants and RKHS norms. It is validated only on a deliberately RKHS-constructed synthetic example; the substantive experiments instead use the standard MLMC allocation. The argument that the MLCF bound is smaller than the CF bound relies on norm inequalities that are asserted rather than established.

The variational-inference extension is not technically convincing. Proposition 3.4 drops the randomness of the accumulated previous gradient and only holds conditionally under vanilla SGD, whereas the experiments use Adam. The scalar theory is not extended rigorously to vector-valued gradients, and the update sign is inconsistent with the stated maximization of the ELBO.

The main MLCFRG experiments use one sample. Under Equation (11), a one-point control-functional estimate algebraically reduces to the raw function evaluation, so these results do not demonstrate any benefit from a control functional unless an unreported estimator was used. A one-sample MLMCRG control is missing.

The ablations contain serious reliability problems: Figures 11 and 12 are identical despite representing different sample-size strategies, and Figures 9/10 duplicate Figures 5/6 despite purportedly changing kernels. This undermines the empirical claims about kernel and sample-size effects.

The cost comparisons count simulator evaluations but omit score computation, kernel construction, cubic linear solves, and hyperparameter optimization. Since the reported simulator costs are only milliseconds, the assertion that this overhead is negligible is particularly doubtful; end-to-end runtime and memory comparisons are needed.

Important reproducibility details are absent, including fidelity step sizes, reference values used for absolute error, MCMC warm-up and mixing diagnostics, several BNN/data-split settings, and numerical regularization values. There are also specification errors, such as an inconsistent sign/scale in the ODE forcing and a Matérn mixed-derivative formula missing dimension factors.

strengths: The method is conceptually clean and potentially useful: it applies Stein control functionals to each correction in a multilevel telescoping estimator and remains applicable to unnormalized target densities.
The paper provides substantive theoretical support, including conditional unbiasedness, a smoothness-dependent variance rate, and a budget-based sample-allocation rule, with proofs in the appendix.

The empirical study is unusually broad, covering synthetic integration, a differential-equation problem, real-data Bayesian inference, and variational inference. Repeated trials, relevant MLMC/CF/MLBQ baselines, and kernel and sampling-design ablations provide credible evidence for the main integration setting.
The presentation is generally organized, and important limitations—dimensionality, smoothness, fidelity construction, and cubic kernel cost—are acknowledged.
weaknesses: The novelty is somewhat incremental: the central construction applies an existing control-functional estimator independently to MLMC corrections, while much of the analysis follows existing single-level bounds plus a standard Lagrange-multiplier allocation. Comparisons with broader multifidelity or approximate-control-variate methods are missing.

The theoretical guarantees have substantially narrower scope than the paper's applicability claims. The finite fill-distance assumption effectively requires a bounded domain with quasi-uniform training points, whereas the Gaussian, posterior-MCMC, and high-dimensional BNN experiments fall outside this regime. Independence across levels should also be stated explicitly.

The proposed allocation minimizes an upper bound involving unknown constants and RKHS norms, not the actual variance. It is validated only on a synthetic integrand constructed from the same kernels, while practical experiments revert to MLMC allocation.

The cost comparisons omit or insufficiently document kernel construction and O(n^3) inversion, score evaluation, and sampling costs. Wall-clock or equal-total-compute results are needed, especially because the demonstrated simulators are inexpensive.

The variational-inference evidence is weak relative to its claims: the main MLCFRG experiments use one sample, for which the simplified control-functional estimate degenerates to the raw sample; MLCFRG is essentially tied with, and sometimes slightly worse than, MLMCRG. Moreover, the efficient update is derived for SGD while the experiments use Adam.

Several confidence-reducing technical and reproducibility inconsistencies remain: the stated Matérn mixed derivative appears to omit a factor of dimension, the per-level marginal-likelihood expression has a log-determinant sign/scale inconsistent with the preceding equation, and the ODE derivation changes the forcing term's sign and magnitude. The estimator variant, reference values used for absolute error, fidelity step sizes, and several BNN data and training details are also insufficiently specified.

strengths: The paper presents a clear and useful synthesis: applying Stein control functionals separately to multilevel corrections combines multifidelity savings with nonparametric variance reduction and supports unnormalized target densities.
The unbiased split estimator, smoothness-dependent variance bound, and cost-constrained sample-allocation result form a coherent theoretical contribution, with reasonably transparent proofs.

Experiments span synthetic integration, differential equations, MCMC-based Bayesian inference, and variational inference. The low-dimensional integration experiments show consistent improvements over MLMC and single-level control functionals, with some kernel, design, and allocation studies.

The manuscript is well organized and visually polished, and it explicitly discusses computational limitations and ethics. Reviewed source: :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/iclr2026--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-9nmjggu0/call-1ed54c84d9394af3a1d86249bf8faf3d/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}
weaknesses: The conceptual novelty is moderate: the estimator applies an existing control-functional construction independently to the standard MLMC telescoping terms, and the principal variance bound largely follows by summing existing single-level bounds. No general theorem establishes improvement over single-level CF; the comparison after Equation 7 relies on unproved norm relationships.

The guarantees require strong conditions—RKHS membership, quasi-uniform training designs, smoothness, and effectively independent i.i.d. samples across levels. The proof uses cross-level independence without stating it clearly. The MCMC experiment, Gaussian-domain examples, and biased simplified estimator do not satisfy the stated framework, substantially weakening the broad-applicability claims.

The variational-inference evidence is particularly unclear. MLCFRG reportedly uses one sample, but Equation 11 reduces exactly to the raw function value when n=1 and is therefore independent of the kernel. The paper does not specify an alternative training/evaluation split that would avoid this degeneracy. Moreover, MLCFRG only matches MLMCRG on test likelihood and is slightly worse for the 20-unit network, so the incremental benefit of control functionals is not demonstrated.

The budget comparisons appear to count model evaluations but not Gram-matrix construction/inversion, score computation, or repeated marginal-likelihood tuning. Given the cubic kernel cost and millisecond-scale simulators, these omissions may materially change the efficiency ranking. The VI comparison by iteration is also not cost-equivalent when methods use different numbers of samples.

Important reproducibility details are missing, including training/test split sizes for CF, regularization values, actual fidelity step sizes, reference values used to compute absolute errors, MCMC diagnostics, and detailed BNN data splits. There are also concrete inconsistencies: the ODE forcing changes from -50^2 x_2^2 to +50x_2^2, and the stated multidimensional Matérn mixed derivative appears to omit dimension factors.

The theoretically derived MLCF allocation is tested only on a favorable synthetic example constructed inside the assumed RKHS; practical experiments instead reuse the MLMC allocation. Thus, a central claimed contribution is not validated under realistic conditions, leaving the overall evidence marginally below the top-tier acceptance threshold.

strengths: The combination of multilevel Monte Carlo telescoping differences with Stein control functionals is natural, potentially useful, and applicable to unnormalized target densities.
The paper gives an explicit conditional variance bound and a cost-constrained sample-allocation rule under stated smoothness and quasi-uniform-design assumptions.
Experiments cover synthetic integration, differential equations, posterior inference, and variational inference, with several relevant baselines and repeated trials.
The presentation is generally clear and acknowledges important limitations such as cubic kernel cost and deterioration with dimension.
weaknesses: The methodological novelty is limited: the construction applies an existing control-functional estimator independently to each MLMC increment, and the rate proof largely sums existing single-level bounds. No valid general result establishes improvement over either MLMC or standard CF; the post-Equation-7 comparisons rely on unproven inequalities between norms in different RKHSs.

The theory has significant gaps. Cross-level independence is required when variances are summed but is not stated. Assumptions A1-A8 are far from mild and are explicitly violated by several experiments. The proposed allocation depends on unknown interpolation constants and RKHS norms; assuming level-dependent constants can be normalized away is unjustified, and practical experiments mostly use the MLMC allocation instead.

The variational-inference extension is insufficiently justified. The scalar RKHS variance result is applied to vector-valued gradients without defining the relevant covariance or function space; the proof conditions on an adaptive trajectory without handling dependence or bias; and Proposition 3.4 assumes vanilla SGD while the experiments use Adam.

The main BNN experiments use one MLCFRG sample. For the presented simplified estimator, a one-point control functional equals the raw function value exactly, so these experiments cannot demonstrate any benefit from the control functional. A same-sample MLMCRG comparison is missing, and Table 6 actually slightly favors MLMCRG.

The budget comparisons omit kernel construction and cubic solves, hyperparameter optimization, score evaluation, and inadequately document MCMC-generation cost. With millisecond-scale simulators and up to 620 samples, these omitted costs may dominate, so the claimed computational efficiency is not established by end-to-end runtime measurements.

There are material correctness and reproducibility problems: the stated Matérn mixed derivative omits the dimension factor in its radial term; the ODE right-hand side changes from -50^2 x_2^2 to +50 x_2^2 in the derivation; the estimator variant used in each experiment and its bias are unclear; reference values used to compute absolute errors are undocumented; and important BNN dataset and likelihood details are missing.

strengths: Addresses an important Monte Carlo variance-reduction problem with a simple and potentially useful combination of multilevel estimation and Stein control functionals.
Provides an unbiased sample-split estimator, a convergence-rate bound inherited across levels, and a principled allocation that minimizes the derived variance upper bound.

Evaluates the method on synthetic integration, differential equations, Bayesian inference with an unnormalized posterior, and variational inference; the repeated integration experiments generally show favorable error trends.

The manuscript is readable and visually organized, and the appendices provide proofs, kernel formulas, and additional experiments. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/iclr2026--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-4lzjtcig/call-1206bb815a3a422488754effb0ff620a/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}
weaknesses: The conceptual novelty is modest: the main estimator applies an existing control-functional construction independently to the standard MLMC telescoping corrections, and much of the theory follows by summing known single-level bounds.

The guarantees rely on strong conditions, including smooth low-dimensional problems, quasi-uniform training designs, and independent IID evaluation samples. The QMC, LHS, MCMC, and adaptive variational-inference experiments fall outside these guarantees. The claimed optimal allocation only optimizes an upper bound and depends on unknown RKHS norms and constants, making it largely impractical outside the constructed synthetic example.

The cost comparisons primarily account for function evaluations while omitting or insufficiently documenting Gram-matrix inversion, hyperparameter optimization, score computation, and sampling costs. Since control-functional fitting is cubic and several reported budgets are below two seconds, matched end-to-end wall-clock comparisons are necessary.

Important controls are missing, including single-level QMC/LHS, CF with the same designs, broader multifidelity control-variate methods, and scalable Stein-control baselines. In the BNN study, methods use different Monte Carlo sample counts, and MLCFRG is only comparable to, and for the 20-unit network slightly worse than, MLMCRG.

Reproducibility is incomplete: the experiments do not clearly specify the training/evaluation split m_l versus n_l, whether the unbiased or simplified biased estimator is used, several fidelity step sizes, reference-value construction, MCMC diagnostics, or sufficient BNN training and data-split details.

There are concerning technical inconsistencies: the stated Matern-5/2 mixed-derivative formula appears to omit dimension factors; the per-level marginal-likelihood expression has a log-determinant sign inconsistent with the preceding objective; and the ODE forcing changes from -50^2 x_2^2 in the main text to +50 x_2^2 in the appendix. The variational derivation is also stated for SGD while the experiments use Adam, without explaining how the estimator or variance result carries over.

strengths: The paper addresses an important problem and presents a simple, broadly useful synthesis of multilevel Monte Carlo with Stein control functionals, including applicability to unnormalized target densities.

The split-sample estimator has a clear unbiasedness argument, a smoothness-dependent variance bound, and a principled cost-constrained sample-allocation result. The main derivations are transparent and technically plausible.

The empirical study is unusually broad: it includes a controlled RKHS example, a boundary-value ODE, Bayesian inference for a Lotka-Volterra model, and Bayesian neural-network variational inference. Comparisons include MLMC, single-level control functionals, Monte Carlo, and multilevel Bayesian quadrature, with consistent gains on the core integration tasks.

The appendices provide useful implementation formulas and ablations over kernels, hyperparameter selection, experimental designs, and sample-size strategies. Limitations and ethical considerations are acknowledged.
weaknesses: The conceptual novelty is moderate: the core estimator applies an existing control-functional construction independently to the corrections in an existing MLMC telescoping sum. Much of the theory follows by summing known control-functional bounds and solving a standard allocation problem, while positioning against broader multifidelity control-variate methods remains limited.

There is a substantial theory-practice gap. The rate requires quasi-uniform training designs, RKHS membership, smoothness and boundary conditions, independent holdout samples, and implicitly independence across levels. The paper explicitly notes that some assumptions fail in its experiments, and it gives no corresponding guarantees for the practical biased all-data estimator or the MCMC setting. Consequently, descriptions such as "mild assumptions" and "broadly applicable" are too strong.

The proposed optimal allocation depends on unknown smoothness, RKHS norms, and constants. It is validated using exact quantities only in a deliberately favorable synthetic construction; the realistic experiments instead use the MLMC allocation. Its practical value is therefore not convincingly established.

The budget comparisons appear to count simulator evaluations while omitting score computation, kernel hyperparameter optimization, and the cubic Gram-matrix solve. End-to-end runtime and memory comparisons are particularly important because these overheads can dominate at the small simulator costs used here. Other missing details include reference-value construction, discretization bias or level selection, Lotka-Volterra step sizes, and MCMC diagnostics.

The variational-inference extension is under-supported. It is tested only on one small dataset and small networks, without wall-clock comparisons or direct gradient-variance measurements; one reported configuration is slightly worse than MLMCRG. Moreover, with the stated single sample, the simplified control-functional estimator reduces algebraically to the raw function value, so the main experiment does not isolate a control-functional benefit. The conditional variance argument also does not establish unconditional behavior along the adaptive optimization trajectory.

strengths: The manuscript :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/iclr2026--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-f8lepwii/call-2aa1bfee6e364e6c8756d22e1e073d40/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"} gives a clean, modular combination of multilevel telescoping estimators and Stein control functionals; with independent sample splitting, the resulting estimator is unbiased and can accommodate unnormalized target densities.
The paper derives a conditional variance bound and a budget-based sample-allocation rule that make the roles of smoothness, dimension, fidelity cost, and inter-level discrepancy explicit.

The empirical study spans synthetic integration, an ODE, posterior integration for a Lotka-Volterra model, and variational inference, with comparisons against MC, MLMC, CF, and—in one experiment—multilevel Bayesian quadrature.
The appendices provide proofs, kernel derivatives, sample allocations, model specifications, and several kernel/sample-size sensitivity experiments.
weaknesses: The conceptual and theoretical novelty is limited: the principal estimator applies an existing control-functional construction independently to each standard MLMC correction, and the main bound follows by summing existing per-level bounds. The proposed allocation also depends on generally unknown RKHS norms and constants and is only directly validated in a synthetic example constructed so those quantities are available.

The theory is poorly aligned with the advertised applications. It requires quasi-uniform fill-distance control, strong RKHS smoothness, Stein boundary conditions, and effectively independent levels; these assumptions fail or are unaddressed for unbounded Gaussian domains, MCMC samples, and high-dimensional variational inference. The claimed comparison showing the MLCF bound below the CF bound additionally relies on unproved norm inequalities and considers only two limiting patterns.

The efficiency comparisons account mainly for model-evaluation budgets while omitting Gram-matrix inversion, repeated kernel-hyperparameter optimization, and target-score evaluation. These costs can dominate here because several reported simulator evaluations take only milliseconds. The neural-network results are plotted against iterations despite methods using different sample counts, with no wall-clock or scaling measurements.

The variational-inference evidence has a particularly serious confound: MLCFRG reportedly uses one sample, but the simplified CF estimator in Equation (11) reduces exactly to the raw function value when n=1. Thus, most reported BNN gains cannot demonstrate an effect from the control functional. Moreover, the scalar fixed-integrand variance theory is applied to vector-valued, adaptively changing gradients without a valid trajectory-level argument.

Important evaluation details are missing or ambiguous, including how reference values for absolute errors were obtained, whether experiments use the unbiased split estimator or the biased simplified estimator, MCMC warm-up/autocorrelation and effective sample sizes, score-computation costs, and precise UCI subsampling/preprocessing/splits. Consequently, the central empirical claims are not sufficiently reproducible or convincingly controlled for a top-tier acceptance.

strengths: The manuscript presents a clean, well-motivated combination of multilevel Monte Carlo and Stein control functionals, including an unbiased split-sample estimator applicable to unnormalized densities. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/iclr2026--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-c9dkgcd4/call-d8bf4f354d32460091972bdb82a385bf/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}
It derives a levelwise variance bound and a closed-form allocation that minimizes this bound under explicit smoothness, RKHS, fill-distance, and cost assumptions.
The low-dimensional integration experiments span synthetic, differential-equation, and Bayesian-inference settings and generally show lower absolute error than MLMC, single-level CF, and MLBQ.
The exposition is accessible, and the appendix provides proofs, several kernel formulas, hyperparameter guidance, and additional experiments.
weaknesses: The variational-inference evidence has a major internal inconsistency: Eq. (11) with the reported single MLCFRG sample reduces exactly to the raw function value and is independent of the kernel; the unbiased estimator cannot be formed from one total sample, and the stated median-distance heuristic is undefined. Consequently, these experiments do not demonstrate a control-functional benefit. Consistently, MLCFRG is only comparable to, and sometimes slightly worse than, MLMCRG in Tables 5–6.

The paper never clearly states which experiments use the unbiased split estimator versus the biased simplified estimator, nor the split ratio. QMC and MCMC experiments fall outside the stated i.i.d. variance theory, so the theoretical guarantees do not support much of the empirical section.

The reported budgets largely count simulator evaluations while omitting Gram-matrix inversion, kernel tuning, score computation, and high-dimensional vector-gradient costs. This is especially problematic for millisecond-scale simulators and the 392/522-dimensional neural networks; no matched end-to-end runtime or memory comparison is provided.

The allocation minimizes a restrictive upper bound involving unknown constants and RKHS norms, not actual MSE. It is validated only on a synthetic function constructed from the same kernels, while practical experiments revert to the MLMC allocation. The argument following Eq. (7) also assumes, without justification, comparisons between RKHS norms and therefore does not establish superiority over CF.

Several technical inconsistencies reduce confidence: the multidimensional Matérn mixed-derivative formula omits dimension factors, the per-level marginal-likelihood expression has an incorrect log-determinant sign/coefficient, Assumption A7 omits level zero although the theorem includes it, and the ODE statement and discretization use inconsistent RHS sign/scale.

Important reproducibility details are missing, including fidelity step sizes for the principal ODE experiments, construction of reference values used for absolute error, MCMC warm-up and diagnostics, randomized-design details, and the wine-data subset, split, and preprocessing. Numerical result tables or confidence intervals are also absent for the main integration studies.

The basic construction and proofs are largely a direct levelwise application of existing control-functional results. Given this incremental novelty and the unresolved validity and evaluation issues above, the submission is not yet competitive at the stated acceptance bar.

strengths: The core idea—applying Stein control functionals separately to multilevel telescoping increments—is intuitive, potentially useful, and broadly compatible with multi-fidelity integration.

The paper gives an unbiased sample-splitting estimator, a convergence bound under explicit smoothness and coverage assumptions, and a sample-allocation derivation. The presentation is generally organized and includes several illustrative applications.

The experiments span synthetic integration, differential-equation models, Bayesian inference, and variational inference, with comparisons to MLMC, single-level control functionals, and multilevel Bayesian quadrature.
weaknesses: The methodological novelty is fairly incremental: the estimator and proof largely compose standard MLMC telescoping, existing control-functional bounds, and a standard Lagrange allocation. No rigorous result establishes improvement over MLMC or CF; the informal comparison to CF assumes unproved inequalities between RKHS norms.

The claimed computational efficiency is not convincingly evaluated. Budgets count simulator evaluations but omit Gram-matrix construction/inversion, kernel hyperparameter optimization, and score evaluations. These costs can be substantial for the reported low-level sample sizes and sub-millisecond simulators, so end-to-end runtime advantages remain unsupported.

There is a major theory–experiment gap. The rate requires quasi-uniform training designs, independent i.i.d. holdout samples, RKHS membership, and finite fill distance. Finite fill distance is impossible on the unbounded Gaussian domains used in several flagship experiments, while the MCMC and biased simplified-estimator settings also fall outside the theorem.

The variational-inference evidence does not isolate the proposed control-functional contribution. MLCFRG uses one sample, for which the simplified CF estimator reduces exactly to the raw function value. The experiments also use Adam although the efficient recursion is derived for SGD, compare against methods using five samples, provide no wall-clock accounting, and show performance essentially tied with MLMCRG.

Reproducibility is inadequate despite the stated claim: important fidelity step sizes, reference values used to compute absolute errors, MCMC configuration, dataset subsampling/splits, estimator variant, and sample-splitting ratios are missing or unclear.

The practical allocation rule depends on unknown RKHS norms and constants and is validated only on a synthetic example constructed from the chosen kernels; real experiments instead reuse MLMC allocations. The variance proof also implicitly needs cross-level independence that is not stated.

strengths: The paper presents an intuitive and potentially useful combination of Stein control functionals with the MLMC telescoping construction, including applicability to unnormalized target densities through score evaluations.
The split-sample estimator is plausibly unbiased, and the paper derives a smoothness- and dimension-dependent variance bound together with a cost-constrained allocation rule.

The empirical section covers several settings—synthetic integration, differential-equation models, posterior inference, and variational inference—and includes repeated trials and relevant basic baselines.
The appendices provide proofs, kernel formulas, and implementation discussion, while the conclusion acknowledges cubic kernel cost, dimensionality, and hierarchy-construction limitations.
weaknesses: The methodological novelty is limited: the core construction applies an existing single-level control-functional estimator independently to each MLMC increment, and the main variance result largely sums existing single-level bounds. The claimed comparison with ordinary CF relies on unproved inequalities between RKHS norms; MLCF and CF have the same asymptotic budget exponent, so no general dominance is established.

The theory requires strong quasi-uniform fill-distance, RKHS-membership, boundary, smoothness, and low-dimensionality assumptions. Assumption A4 is especially unrealistic as written for all auxiliary distributions, A7 omits the level-zero integrand, and cross-level independence is not clearly assumed. The Gaussian, MCMC, and high-dimensional BNN experiments do not satisfy the stated theory. Moreover, the analysis fixes f_L=f and omits the discretization-bias/level-selection analysis central to practical MLMC.

Proposition 3.4 removes the variance and covariance contributed by the random previous update lambda_L-lambda_{L-1}; its bound is defensible only after conditioning on the complete optimization history, not as the displayed variance claim. The adaptive trajectory also prevents direct application of Theorem 3.2 without additional analysis. In the main BNN experiments, MLCFRG uses one sample; for the simplified estimator in Equation 11, a one-point control functional algebraically reduces to the raw function value, so these experiments do not demonstrate a benefit from the control-functional component.

Efficiency comparisons constrain only simulator-evaluation cost while omitting Gram-matrix inversion, kernel evaluation, and hyperparameter optimization. These costs may dominate for the reported millisecond-scale simulators, yet no wall-clock or scaling results are given. Strong alternatives such as multilevel QMC are also absent, and the theoretically proposed MLCF allocation is tested only on a synthetic problem constructed from the same RKHS used by the method.

Reproducibility is insufficient at several important points: it is unclear which experiments use the unbiased split estimator versus the biased simplified estimator; ground-truth integral calculations are unspecified; ODE and Lotka–Volterra level step sizes and MCMC diagnostics are missing; synthetic numerical budgets are not reported; and the BNN data split, preprocessing, observation model, and cost-matched protocol are under-described. The 20-unit BNN results are essentially tied with, or slightly worse than, MLMCRG.

There are concrete technical inconsistencies in the implementation appendix: the Matern-2.5 mixed-derivative trace is missing a factor of the dimension d, the per-level marginal-likelihood expression has the wrong sign/scaling for the log-determinant term, and the ODE forcing changes sign and magnitude between its definition and discretization. These errors undermine confidence in reproducibility and possibly in the corresponding experiments.

strengths: The paper presents a useful and conceptually clean combination of multilevel Monte Carlo with Stein control functionals, including an unbiased sample-splitting estimator applicable to unnormalized target densities.
The conditional variance bound and budget-constrained sample allocation are clearly stated, with derivations provided in the appendix and explicit dependence on smoothness and dimension.

The empirical study spans synthetic integration, differential equations, Bayesian inference, and variational inference. The numerical-integration experiments repeatedly compare against MLMC and single-level control functionals and include several kernel and sampling-design ablations.
The manuscript is generally readable, acknowledges important limitations, and supplies substantial implementation and experimental detail.
weaknesses: The methodological novelty is fairly incremental: the main estimator applies an existing control-functional estimator independently to each MLMC correction, while the principal bound and allocation rule largely follow by summing existing per-level results and applying a standard Lagrange-multiplier argument.

The theory relies on restrictive conditions—quasi-uniform training points, exact RKHS membership, smoothness, boundary conditions, and independent evaluation samples—that are violated by several headline experiments involving QMC, LHS, MCMC, and unbounded posteriors. The biased simplified estimator enabling arbitrary designs receives no corresponding bias or MSE analysis, and the paper does not clearly report which estimator or train/evaluation split is used in each experiment.

The reported budgets appear to count simulator evaluations but not Gram-matrix inversion, kernel hyperparameter optimization, score computation, or memory. Since fitting scales cubically and several simulators are inexpensive, the experiments do not establish an advantage in total wall-clock cost.

The proposed optimal allocation requires unknown smoothness, constants, and RKHS norms. It is demonstrated only on a deliberately favorable synthetic construction where these norms are analytic; the practical experiments instead use the MLMC allocation. Comparisons to broader multifidelity/approximate-control-variate methods and empirical convergence-rate studies are also missing.

The variational-inference evidence is not convincing. It covers one dataset and small networks, compares methods using different Monte Carlo sample counts on an iteration rather than compute axis, and reports parity or slightly worse performance than MLMCRG in one setting. Moreover, with one sample the simplified control-functional estimator algebraically reduces to the raw one-sample correction, so the experiments do not isolate a benefit from the control functional. The scalar, conditional SGD analysis is also not reconciled with vector gradients and the use of Adam.

Several reproducibility and correctness issues remain: the ODE forcing changes from −50²x₂² to +50x₂² in the appendix derivation, the stated Matérn mixed derivative omits dimension factors, and the per-level marginal-likelihood expression has a sign/parenthesization inconsistent with the preceding objective. Ground-truth construction, fidelity step sizes, MCMC diagnostics, and important BNN details are insufficiently specified.

strengths: The manuscript :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/iclr2026--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-n6zip6t1/call-f8c5e883060b42b68c8e2defb1e0c728/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"} presents a clean, useful construction: applying Stein control functionals separately to the corrections in a multilevel Monte Carlo decomposition, while retaining applicability to unnormalized targets through score evaluations.

The split-sample estimator is unbiased under the stated conditions, and the paper provides a level-wise variance bound, a faster asymptotic rate for smooth low-dimensional problems, and a closed-form allocation under a fixed evaluation budget. The proofs are largely self-contained.

The empirical study spans synthetic integration, a differential-equation problem, Bayesian inference with real ecological data, and variational inference for Bayesian neural networks. Comparisons against MC, MLMC, single-level CF, and MLBQ generally favor MLCF on the integration tasks.
The motivation and presentation are clear, with useful implementation appendices, kernel/design sensitivity experiments, explicit limitations, and appropriate ethics and LLM-use disclosures.
weaknesses: The conceptual novelty is moderate: the main estimator is a direct composition of an existing control-functional estimator with the standard MLMC telescoping sum. Much of the analysis follows by summing known single-level bounds and applying a Lagrange multiplier. No rigorous condition establishes when MLCF improves over CF or MLMC; the informal comparison after Equation 7 relies on unproved RKHS-norm inequalities across different spaces.

There is a substantial theory-to-experiment gap. The guarantees require smooth functions, quasi-uniform training designs, and i.i.d. independent level estimators, and the fill-distance condition is not meaningful on the unbounded Gaussian domains used in several experiments. They therefore do not cover the MCMC, QMC/LHS, high-dimensional, or adaptive variational-inference settings. Proposition 3.4 bounds only conditional variance, while the claim about the full stochastic optimization trajectory does not follow directly from Theorem 3.2.

The budget comparisons are not convincingly end-to-end: the paper does not report whether cubic kernel fitting, score computation, hyperparameter optimization, or pilot estimation for MLMC allocation are included. Wall-clock measurements are absent, and the proposed MLCF allocation is evaluated only on the synthetic example using known RKHS norms.

The Bayesian-neural-network evidence is especially weak. With one sample, the simplified estimator in Equation 11 algebraically reduces to the raw single-sample correction, so those experiments cannot demonstrate a benefit from the control functional itself. They also compare one MLCFRG sample with five samples for competing estimators without matched runtime; on the 20-unit network, MLCFRG is slightly worse than MLMCRG in both reported metrics.

Important reproducibility details are missing, including which split versus simplified estimator is used in each experiment, the split ratio, reference values used to compute absolute error, practical ODE/Lotka-Volterra level step sizes, MCMC diagnostics, and the BNN subsampling and data split. There are also technical inconsistencies: the per-level marginal-likelihood expression has the wrong log-determinant sign relative to the preceding expression, the Matérn mixed derivative omits dimension-dependent terms for d>1, and the ODE forcing changes from -50^2 x_2^2 to +50 x_2^2. These issues make a score above the acceptance threshold difficult despite the promising core idea.

Please serve as an expert reviewer for a top-tier AI conference with an acceptance rate of about 30%.
Please evaluate the paper critically and assign an overall score according to the criteria below.

Assign an Overall Assessment (OA) score according to the rating scale below.
Choose an OA score from: 1, 3, 5, 6, 8, or 10.

Rating scale:
1 = Strong Reject
A paper with fundamental problems such as well-known or trivial results, serious technical flaws, unsupported central claims, invalid evaluation, or unaddressed ethical concerns.

3 = Reject
A paper that is not competitive for a top-tier AI conference due to meaningful weaknesses in novelty, technical soundness, evaluation, reproducibility, clarity, significance, or positioning.
A paper can receive 3 even if it is understandable, technically plausible, or has some strengths, if the overall contribution or evidence is insufficient.

5 = Marginally below the acceptance threshold
A technically solid paper with some positive qualities, but where the reasons for a lower score slightly outweigh the reasons for a higher score.
Typical reasons include limited novelty, incomplete evaluation, weak or missing baselines, insufficient ablations, unclear significance, narrow scope, limited reproducibility, or claims that are stronger than the evidence.
Please use sparingly.

6 = Marginally above the acceptance threshold
A technically solid paper where the reasons for a higher score clearly outweigh the weaknesses.
A rating of 6 requires concrete positive evidence that the paper is competitive for a top-tier AI conference, such as a clear contribution, convincing evaluation, appropriate baselines, and sufficient support for the main claims.
Do not assign 6 merely because the paper is coherent, plausible, or has some positive results.
Please use sparingly.

8 = Accept
A strong paper with a clear and meaningful contribution, convincing technical quality, good-to-excellent evaluation, appropriate comparisons, sufficient reproducibility, and clear relevance to the field.
The paper should have high impact on at least one sub-area of AI or moderate-to-high impact on more than one area of AI.
Minor weaknesses are acceptable, but there should be no major unresolved issues in soundness, evaluation, novelty, or ethics.

10 = Strong Accept
An exceptional paper with groundbreaking impact on one or more areas of AI, technically excellent work, exceptionally strong evaluation, strong reproducibility and resources, and no unaddressed ethical considerations.
This rating should be reserved for rare submissions that are clearly among the best papers in the venue.

Output Format

Provide your review in JSON format. Use a numeric value for oa and lists of text for strengths and weaknesses:

{"oa": <num>, "strengths": ["<text>"], "weaknesses": ["<text>"]}

strengths: The core idea is intuitive and useful: applying Stein control functionals separately to multilevel telescoping increments can combine two complementary forms of variance reduction. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/iclr2026--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-q7axwpay/call-4dff674f6ba84ed19e0c5c99cc149416/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}
The paper provides an unbiased split-sample estimator, a smoothness-dependent variance bound, and a cost-constrained allocation derived from that bound.
The empirical section spans synthetic integration, differential equations, an unnormalized Bayesian posterior, and variational inference, with multiple kernels and experimental designs.
The manuscript is generally readable, includes proofs and implementation material, acknowledges important limitations, and raises no evident unaddressed ethical concern.
weaknesses: The theory-to-practice gap is substantial. The main guarantees require i.i.d. evaluation samples, quasi-uniform training designs, Stein boundary conditions, and effectively cross-level independence, whereas prominent experiments use QMC, LHS, and correlated MCMC samples and explicitly admit that assumptions are violated. The biased simplified estimator appears necessary in several experiments, but the estimator variant and train/evaluation split used in each result are not specified.

The budget comparisons account primarily for integrand evaluations while omitting kernel fitting and inversion, score computation, hyperparameter optimization, and MCMC generation. This is especially problematic because the method costs O(m^3), sample counts reach hundreds, and the showcased integrands have millisecond-scale costs. Consequently, the claimed computational-efficiency advantage is not established by end-to-end runtime or equal-compute comparisons.

The absolute-error experiments never define how the reference integrals were obtained. Important reproducibility details are also absent, including fidelity step sizes for several experiments, MCMC warm-up/autocorrelation diagnostics, QMC randomization, regularization values, and uncertainty or statistical tests for method comparisons.

The allocation is optimal only for an upper bound under common smoothness and split-ratio assumptions and depends on unknown RKHS norms and constants. It is demonstrated only on an example deliberately constructed from kernel sections; practical experiments instead reuse the MLMC allocation, leaving a central claimed contribution weakly validated.

The variational-inference extension is not convincing: the recurrence is derived for SGD but evaluated with Adam, no optimization guarantee is given, and only one small UCI task is tested. MLCFRG uses one sample while baselines use five without wall-clock normalization; moreover, a one-point simplified scalar control-functional estimate collapses to the raw function value, so these experiments do not clearly isolate any benefit from control functionals. Results are essentially tied with, and sometimes slightly worse than, MLMCRG.

There are concrete technical and reproducibility inconsistencies. The ODE changes from a right-hand side of -50^2 x_2^2 to +50 x_2^2 in its expansion and discretization; the stated isotropic Matérn mixed-derivative formula appears to omit dimension factors; and the variance proof sums level variances without explicitly assuming independence across levels.

The novelty is a relatively direct composition of established MLMC and control-functional estimators. Comparisons omit broader multifidelity/control-variate and scalable Stein-control alternatives, so the evidence does not yet show sufficient novelty or robustness for a top-tier acceptance.

strengths: The paper offers a coherent and potentially useful combination of multilevel Monte Carlo and Stein control functionals, enabling variance reduction for unnormalized targets encountered in Bayesian computation.
The conditional unbiasedness result, levelwise variance bound, and budget-allocation analysis provide a meaningful theoretical foundation, with assumptions and proofs presented explicitly.

The evaluation covers synthetic integration, a boundary-value ODE, real-data Lotka-Volterra inference, and Bayesian neural-network variational inference. Relevant baselines include MLMC, standard control functionals, multilevel Bayesian quadrature, and MLMCRG, and the core integration experiments show substantial error reductions.
The manuscript is generally well organized and clearly motivates its relevance to probabilistic computation and machine learning.
weaknesses: The computational-budget comparisons count integrand evaluations but apparently omit Gram-matrix construction and inversion, score computation, and kernel-hyperparameter optimization. With cubic kernel cost, hundreds of coarse-level samples, and reported budgets below two seconds, this omission undermines the claimed end-to-end efficiency.

The theoretical assumptions do not match several experiments: the rate requires quasi-uniform training designs and independent test samples, whereas experiments use IID or dependent MCMC samples; the high-dimensional ReLU BNN setting also conflicts with the smooth, low-dimensional RKHS regime. The experiments appear to use the biased all-sample estimator, but the resulting bias and exact estimator choice are not clearly reported.

The variational-inference evidence has a serious issue: with the stated single sample, the simplified control-functional estimator in Equation (11) algebraically reduces to the raw one-sample gradient, independently of the kernel. Moreover, Proposition 3.4 is derived for SGD while the experiments use Adam, and the tables show no consistent advantage over MLMCRG.

The proposed optimal allocation depends on unknown RKHS norms and constants and is demonstrated only on a synthetic integrand constructed from the same RKHS. Practical experiments instead reuse the MLMC allocation, leaving this contribution weakly validated.

Important implementation and evaluation details are missing, including reference values used to compute absolute errors, fidelity step sizes, MCMC diagnostics, data splits, and estimator splitting parameters. There are also apparent technical inconsistencies in the appendix, including a dimensionally incorrect Matérn mixed derivative, conflicting marginal-likelihood formulas, and inconsistent sign/scale in the ODE forcing term.

Overall, the central construction is promising but fairly incremental, and the unresolved cost accounting, theory-experiment mismatch, and problematic variational-inference validation place the paper slightly below the top-tier acceptance threshold.

strengths: The manuscript presents a clear and useful idea: apply Stein control functionals separately to the corrections in an MLMC telescoping sum. The resulting method is intuitive and broadly relevant to expensive integration problems. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/iclr2026--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-u9r77g84/call-8c5ebb584266455aa6d9ecb632bdb057/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

The split-sample estimator is unbiased under the required Stein and independence conditions, and the paper derives a meaningful RKHS-based conditional variance bound and a closed-form allocation minimizing that bound.
The Stein construction permits unnormalized target densities and can be combined with experimental designs such as QMC and Latin hypercube sampling, giving the method potentially broad applicability.

The experiments cover synthetic integration, differential equations, Bayesian inference, and variational inference. Repeated-trial comparisons against MLMC, single-level control functionals, MLBQ, MCMC, and MLMCRG generally demonstrate improved accuracy per simulator-evaluation budget.
weaknesses: The conceptual novelty is limited: the estimator is essentially a direct composition of existing control functionals with the standard MLMC telescoping decomposition, while the main bound and allocation argument largely reuse established per-level CF analysis and standard Lagrange allocation. Positioning against broader multifidelity control-variate methods is incomplete.

The theory has a substantial mismatch with the experiments. The fill-distance assumption cannot hold for finite designs on the unbounded Gaussian and posterior domains used in several experiments; cross-level independence is needed but not stated; and QMC, LHS, and MCMC settings do not satisfy the stated i.i.d. assumptions. The paper even notes that some assumptions fail, but supplies no alternative guarantees.

Reported budgets appear to omit cubic Gram-matrix fitting, score evaluation, and repeated kernel-hyperparameter optimization. These costs may dominate for the listed sub-millisecond simulators and hundreds of low-level samples. Without end-to-end runtime or memory comparisons, the central computational-efficiency claim is not convincingly established.

The variational-inference extension has unresolved soundness and evidence issues. Its update sign is inconsistent with the stated maximization of the ELBO, and the variance derivation discards randomness and covariance from previous adaptive iterates unless interpreted only conditionally. No optimization convergence analysis is provided. Moreover, the principal results are essentially tied with MLMCRG, and with one sample the simplified CF estimator degenerates to the raw one-sample estimate.

Important implementation details are absent, including whether experiments use the unbiased or simplified biased estimator, the training/evaluation split ratio, several fidelity step sizes, regularization values, MCMC diagnostics, and how reference integrals for absolute-error plots were obtained. This weakens reproducibility and obscures the connection between theory and experiments.

There are concrete technical inconsistencies in the appendix: the mixed derivative of the Matérn-2.5 kernel omits the dimension factor in general dimension, the supposedly equivalent per-level marginal-likelihood objective has the wrong log-determinant sign/factor, and the ODE forcing changes sign or scale during discretization. These errors further reduce confidence in reproducibility.

The proposed optimal allocation depends on unknown RKHS norms and constants. It is validated only on a specially constructed synthetic example, where the MLMC allocation is sometimes as good or better, while realistic experiments revert to MLMC allocations. Thus its practical value is not demonstrated.

strengths: The paper presents a natural and potentially useful synthesis: applying Stein control functionals to each correction in an MLMC telescoping sum. The exposition is generally readable and the estimator is easy to understand. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/iclr2026--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-ss9i7i8m/call-ecd2dd5be71344c9927920a4eac86926/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

Under the stated split-sample and Stein assumptions, the unbiasedness argument is sensible. The paper also derives a conditional variance bound and a closed-form budget allocation exposing the roles of smoothness, dimension, level cost, and increment RKHS norm.

The empirical section spans synthetic integration, a boundary-value problem, posterior integration, and variational inference. The low-dimensional experiments generally indicate lower absolute error than MC, MLMC, CF, and, where included, multilevel Bayesian quadrature.

The appendices provide derivations, kernel formulas, sample allocations, and several ablations. Limitations such as cubic Gram-matrix cost, smoothness dependence, and the need for a fidelity hierarchy are acknowledged, and no material ethical concern is apparent.
weaknesses: The conceptual novelty is limited: the principal estimator is a sum of existing single-level control-functional estimators, while the variance proof applies a known interpolation result levelwise and the allocation uses a standard Lagrange-multiplier calculation. Positioning against broader multifidelity/approximate-control-variate methods is incomplete.

The theory supports much less than the broad claims suggest. It requires strong RKHS membership, boundary/Stein conditions, quasi-uniform training designs, and independent i.i.d. evaluation sets; the equality between the variance of the sum and the sum of variances also needs cross-level independence that is not stated. The MCMC and VI settings do not meet these conditions, and the appendix explicitly concedes that some experiments violate the assumptions.

No theorem actually guarantees improvement over single-level CF. The argument that the MLCF bound is smaller assumes favorable, unverified inequalities between RKHS norms belonging to different spaces. Moreover, the proposed allocation depends on unknown norms and constants and is meaningfully validated only on a synthetic integrand constructed directly from the chosen kernels.

The experiments apparently use the biased all-sample estimator of Eq. 11—sample-split sizes or the ratio rho are never reported—but do not clearly identify this choice or quantify its bias. Computational budgets omit score computation, O(n^3) kernel solves, and marginal-likelihood tuning, despite computational efficiency being central. Ground-truth construction for the reported absolute errors, MCMC diagnostics, end-to-end runtimes, and statistical significance tests are also missing.

The VI evidence has serious internal inconsistencies. Proposition 3.4 derives its recursion only for plain SGD, whereas the experiments use Adam. More importantly, the reported MLCFRG sample size is one: under Eq. 11, a one-point control-functional estimate algebraically equals the raw function value, so the kernel cancels and a pairwise-distance median heuristic is undefined. A different reuse scheme, if used, is undocumented. The main numerical results are only a near tie with MLMCRG for 15 hidden units and slightly worse for 20 units, so they do not convincingly support the claimed CF-based benefit.

Reproducibility is further weakened by missing fidelity step sizes, split rules, regularization values, hyperparameter-optimization details, data splits, and chain settings. There are consequential formula inconsistencies: the ODE right-hand side changes from -50^2 x_2^2 to +50 x_2^2, the stated Matérn-2.5 mixed derivative omits dimension factors, and the per-level marginal-likelihood expression has a different log-determinant sign/scale from the preceding supposedly equivalent objective. Taken together, these are too substantial for a borderline acceptance, although the core integration idea remains plausible.
